newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia denies drug lord extradition to U.S..
newsitem.headline: Colombia denies drug lord extradition to U.S..

text.p: President Ernesto Samper's government has denied a U.S. request for the extradition of four Cali drug cartel kingpins, Colombia's CM& television news network reported on Thursday.

Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia cited a constitutional ban on extradition passed by the Colombian Congress in 1991 as the sole reason for rejecting the request made in June by U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno, the network said.
Mejia said in a letter to Colombia's chief prosecutor that the ban took precedence over a 1979 U.S.-Colombia extradition treaty, even though the treaty was still in effect, it said.

Officials at the Foreign Ministry and the office of Prosecutor-General Alfonso Valdivieso, a popular anti-drug crusader favored by the United States, could not be reached for immediate comment on the report.

Brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the Cali cartel kingpins who U.S. officials say once controlled up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade, were jailed in 1995 during a nationwide sweep against their criminal drug empire.

Judicial sources said the two reputed billionaires will probably be sentenced to no more than 8 to 12 years in Colombia because of plea bargaining agreements and the country's lenient penalties for drug trafficking.
Reno's request also called for the extradition of Helmer Herrera, considered the No. 3 man in the Cali cartel, and Juan Carlos Abadia, a cartel enforcer known as "Lollipop."
Colombia's Congress is currently debating a bill that would lift the country's ban on extradition.

But a majority of lawmakers appear set against any move to reinstate the practice retroactively, meaning that the Rodriguez Orejuelas and their underlings are unlikely to be punished for any crimes committed outside of Colombia.

Samper, whose 1994 election campaign is alleged to have received millions of dollars in contributions from the Cali cartel, has not backed lifting the extradition ban and instead calls for stiffer penalities for drug barons punished at home.
